name: Progressive macular hypomelanosis
aliases: progressive macular hypomelanosis of the trunk

clinicalPearls: Ill-defined, non-scaly, nummular hypopigmented macules concentrated on the trunk, particularly the central back and chest, in young adults
Follicular red fluorescence under Wood lamp reflects porphyrin-producing Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium) acnes within the follicles
Frequently mistaken for pityriasis versicolor, but potassium hydroxide microscopy is negative for fungal elements
More common in young women and in tropical or warmer climates
The hypopigmentation is functional rather than destructive, with melanocytes preserved but producing less melanin
Antimicrobial and light-based treatments directed at the follicular organism, including targeted ultraviolet phototherapy, can encourage repigmentation
Tends to run a chronic course with a tendency to relapse
reference.pathophysiology: A particular strain of follicular Cutibacterium acnes is thought to produce a factor that interferes with melanogenesis, reducing melanin output without destroying melanocytes; this explains the hypopigmentation rather than depigmentation and the characteristic follicular porphyrin fluorescence. The lack of scale and negative fungal microscopy separate it from pityriasis versicolor. The condition is not primarily an inflammatory or autoimmune process.
additionalInvestigations: Wood-lamp examination for follicular red fluorescence
Potassium hydroxide microscopy, which is negative for fungal hyphae
Dermoscopy to assess the hypopigmented pattern
Sensory examination to exclude leprosy in endemic areas
Skin biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: An anaesthetic patch or thickened peripheral nerve suggesting leprosy in endemic settings
Atypical, rapidly spreading or persistently symptomatic lesions
Failure to respond to appropriate therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but chronic and relapsing; repigmentation may follow treatment and some cases improve spontaneously over years, though recurrence is common.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating it as pityriasis versicolor despite negative microscopy
Overlooking hypopigmented leprosy in endemic populations
Expecting a rapid response, when repigmentation is typically slow
Confusing it with vitiligo or idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis
management: Antimicrobial therapy directed at follicular Cutibacterium acnes, using topical benzoyl peroxide and clindamycin and, where needed, an oral tetracycline-class antibiotic
Ultraviolet phototherapy such as narrowband UVB, often combined with antimicrobials, to stimulate repigmentation
Reassure the patient about the benign, non-scarring nature and set expectations for slow repigmentation and possible relapse
Distinguish from pityriasis versicolor and avoid ineffective antifungal treatment given the negative potassium hydroxide microscopy
Monitor response and re-treat relapses, as recurrence is common while some cases improve spontaneously over years
Dermatology referral for diagnostic confirmation and access to phototherapy
